claims.text: Mechanical-property differences among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets originate from differences in short-range order and nanocluster formation.
Compositional complexity controls the extent and spatial distribution of SRO and nanoclusters.
The equiatomic quinary alloy has an optimal, intermediate level of SRO.
SRO in the equiatomic quinary alloy pins dislocations and thereby increases yield strength.
Reducing the number of constituents from five to four or three alters or suppresses SRO formation.
The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy can have a single-phase FCC structure under suitable processing conditions.
The quaternary and ternary derivatives can all be processed into single-phase FCC structures using the stated standard thermomechanical treatment.
Applying identical thermomechanical schedules and deformation conditions will ensure that all tested alloys remain single-phase FCC.
Changing constituent count modifies chemical-ordering kinetics during thermomechanical processing.
Dominant local chemical order can increase dislocation activation barriers, make dislocation lines wavier, and raise critical resolved shear stress.
The equiatomic quinary alloy deforms through a mixture of dislocation slip and mechanical twinning.
SRO is responsible for influencing the balance between slip and twinning in the equiatomic quinary alloy.
Simpler quaternary and ternary alloys have less dislocation pinning because their SRO is suppressed or modified.
Quaternary and ternary subsets will have lower nanocluster density than the equiatomic quinary baseline.
Quaternary and ternary subsets will have SRO patterns different from those of the equiatomic quinary baseline.
Diminished SRO should produce lower yield strength.
Differences in SRO should produce changes in strain-hardening behavior.
Differences in SRO may produce changes in strain-rate sensitivity.
The hypothesis is restricted to alloys retained as stable, single-phase FCC materials under substantially standardized processing.

The hypothesis is falsified if SRO or nanocluster differences fail to correlate with the predicted mechanical differences, or if simulations show that changing SRO alone cannot account for those differences.
